page: Microsoft Azure D96lds_v7 is a compute-optimized virtual machine from the Dldsv7 family, running on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. It features 96 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 48 physical cores of an Intel Xeon 6973P-C processor operating at 4.2 GHz. The system is equipped with 192.0 GB of system memory, yielding a low memory-to-vCPU ratio of 2.0 GB per core. It includes 5669 GB of local storage and is Premium Storage capable, though it does not bundle any complimentary public IPv4 addresses or GPU hardware.

Performance benchmarks indicate strong multi-core capabilities, with a stress-ng multi-core score of 100098.18 and a PassMark CPU score of 108246.31. The processor's advanced instruction sets, including AVX-512 and Intel AMX (Advanced Matrix Extensions), contribute to top-tier performance in extended instructions, encryption, and physics simulations. Memory bandwidth is highly efficient, reaching 7403.16 GB/sec for cached small-block reads and 349.97 GB/sec for uncached large-block reads. Single-threaded performance is moderate, as shown by average stress-ng single-core results, but multi-threaded decompression and compression tasks, such as bzip3, achieve top-tier throughput.

This server is highly cost-efficient for compute-heavy workloads that do not require massive memory footprints, maximizing CPU density per resource. The inclusion of 5669 GB of local storage makes it suitable for high-throughput database operations, as evidenced by top-tier PassMark database and Redis SET performance. It is also well-suited for static web serving, multi-threaded data processing, and CPU-based machine learning inference, where its AMX-driven prompt processing speeds reach top-tier levels.

The architecture supports advanced instruction sets like AVX-512 and Intel AMX, which accelerate cryptography, physics simulations, and CPU-based LLM prompt processing. With its high compute-to-memory ratio and substantial local storage, the D96lds_v7 is highly cost-efficient for database operations, multi-threaded data decompression, static web serving, and high-density compute workloads.
